title: Banda Hit 48.2°C on Tuesday. Across North India, the Heat Is Killing People and Breaking the Power Grid.
excerpt: At least 18 dead, a record 257 GW in power demand, and the monsoon still days away — India's 2026 heatwave is not slowing down.
body:
The numbers are brutal and they are getting worse. On Tuesday, the small city of Banda in Uttar Pradesh recorded a maximum temperature of 48.2 degrees Celsius — the highest in the state and among the hottest readings anywhere on the planet this week. It was the second time this month that Banda topped India's temperature charts.

Across Uttar Pradesh, mercury crossed 40°C in 22 of the state's 75 districts. But the crisis is not confined to one state. The India Meteorological Department has issued heatwave warnings covering at least ten states, including Delhi, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh. In several pockets, "severe heatwave" conditions — defined as temperatures exceeding normal by more than 6.4°C — have been declared.

The IMD has now issued a red alert for Uttar Pradesh for 20 and 21 May, with an orange alert for western UP extending through 26 May.

## The Death Toll Is Mounting

At least 18 people have died from heat-related causes in recent days, according to reports collated by multiple news agencies. The real toll is almost certainly higher: India has historically undercounted heat deaths because many victims — agricultural labourers, construction workers, street vendors — die in settings where no autopsy is conducted and no formal cause of death is recorded. A broader accounting places suspected heatstroke cases between March and May 2026 at over 25,000 across the country, with at least 56 confirmed fatalities in that wider window.

The worst-hit states are Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, where temperatures have hovered between 45°C and 48°C for days on end. In parts of Madhya Pradesh, stations recorded readings approaching 48°C — nearly 118°F.

## The Grid Is Groaning

The human toll has a mirror in infrastructure. On Monday, India's peak power demand hit a fresh all-time record of 257.37 gigawatts at 3:42 pm, surpassing the previous high of 256.1 GW set just last month. The power ministry said demand was met "without any shortfall," but the margin is razor-thin. During non-solar hours — when solar panels stop generating and coal and gas plants carry the entire load — demand also hit a new high of 247.21 GW at 10:29 pm.

The strain is visible across daily life. Extended school closures have been declared across Delhi, UP, Haryana, and Bihar. States including Rajasthan and Punjab have shifted school schedules to morning-only sessions. Construction activity in several cities has been restricted during peak afternoon hours. Water tanker demand in Delhi has surged as the Yamuna sits at its lowest summer levels in years.

## The Monsoon Is Close — But Not Close Enough

The IMD says the southwest monsoon is likely to reach Kerala by 26 May, roughly on schedule, with a model error margin of plus or minus four days. But for the scorched plains of the Hindi heartland, meaningful relief is still weeks away. The monsoon typically reaches Delhi and UP only by late June.

Until then, the IMD has forecast heatwave to severe heatwave conditions across north and central India through at least 25 May. Rajasthan is expected to remain under heatwave conditions for the entire week. Coastal Andhra Pradesh may face severe heatwave episodes on 21 and 22 May.

## Why This Matters for NRIs

For the millions of diaspora Indians with parents, grandparents, and extended family in UP, Rajasthan, Delhi, and Bihar, these are not abstract climate statistics. They are the daily reality of elderly relatives in homes that often lack air conditioning, of villages where power cuts coincide with the hottest hours, and of farm communities whose livelihoods depend on surviving the brutal weeks between May and the arrival of the rains.

The 2026 heatwave has arrived earlier and hit harder than in most recent years. With climate projections suggesting this pattern will intensify, the question for Indian policymakers — and for the diaspora organisations that increasingly fund rural infrastructure and healthcare — is no longer whether to act, but how fast.
